ROADMAP

Power is a mission resource, not just a subsystem

Core design question: Can the spacecraft deliver the required power when each load needs it, through every mission mode, at end of life, with margin?
WattsPeak power sizes converters, switches and wiring.
Watt-hoursEnergy per orbit sizes the array and the battery.
YearsMission life sets degradation, cycle count and margin.
2 / 54
Study notes

The seven boxes are the order of work for any electrical power system (EPS) design, and they are also the order of this lecture. The dashed arrow matters: every time a load, the thermal design or the schedule changes, you go round again.

Keep the three tiles in mind for every calculation that follows. Watts size converters, switches and wiring. Watt-hours size the array and the battery. Years set degradation, cycle count and margin.

Check yourself. Which quantity sizes the battery: the peak power in W or the eclipse energy in Wh?

The eclipse energy in Wh. Peak power sizes the converters, switches and wiring that must carry it.

Slide 3
ROADMAP · SYSTEMS VIEW

The EPS closes a spacecraft-level resource loop

  • Orbit/attitude determine illumination, eclipse, pointing losses and radiation degradation.
  • Payload/comms determine average and peak electrical demand.
  • Thermal can become the dominant eclipse load through heaters.
  • Operations decide which loads are simultaneous and therefore whether the design closes.
The EPS budget is therefore a mission-operations model expressed in watts and watt-hours.
3 / 54
Study notes

The EPS sits in the centre because each of the four neighbours sets part of its size. Orbit and attitude give the sunlight and eclipse times, the Sun angle and the radiation dose. Payload and comms give the average and peak demand. Thermal adds heater load, mostly in eclipse. Operations decide which loads run at the same time.

The dashed arrows are what the EPS gives back: bus power to every subsystem, and telemetry (voltage, current, temperature, state of charge) for fault detection.

Slide 5
1 · REQUIREMENTS

Mission requirements flow down into EPS requirements

  • Mission objectives define what must operate and when.
  • Orbit defines sunlight/eclipses, radiation and thermal environment.
  • Mission life drives EOL degradation and cycle count.
  • Spacecraft architecture defines bus voltage, peak loads, redundancy and deployment constraints.
5 / 54
Study notes

Read the diagram from top to bottom. Each level is derived from the one above it, so every EPS requirement should trace back to a mission need. The EPS requirements at the bottom are exactly the quantities you will calculate in this lecture: the power profile, the margin, the bus voltage, the battery size and the end-of-life array power.

Check yourself. Which mission-level decision sets the number of battery charge cycles?

The orbit (how many eclipses per year) together with the mission length.

Slide 6
1 · DEFINITIONS

Power and energy answer different questions

\[P=\frac{dE}{dt}\quad [W],\qquad E=\int P(t)\,dt\quad [Wh]\]
  • Power determines whether the source, converter, wiring and switch can support an instantaneous load.
  • Energy determines how long storage can sustain a load.
  • A 100 W transmitter for 6 minutes uses only 10 Wh, but the EPS must still deliver 100 W while it is on.
Mission-design implication

Average power sizes generation over time. Peak power sizes buses, converters and switching. Eclipse energy sizes the battery.

6 / 54
Study notes

Power is a rate; energy is the area under the power-time curve. The chart shows two loads with the same area, 10 Wh, and very different heights. The tall one needs a 100 W converter and wiring. The wide one needs only 10 W of hardware but runs ten times as long.

Worked example. A 100 W transmitter runs for 6 minutes. Energy = 100 × 6 ÷ 60 = 10 Wh. The EPS must still deliver 100 W while it is on.
Check yourself. A 45 W transmitter runs for 12 minutes in each 96-minute orbit. Find its energy per orbit and its contribution to orbit-average power.

Energy = 45 × 12 ÷ 60 = 9 Wh. Average contribution = 45 × 12 ÷ 96 = 5.6 W.

1 · POWER PROFILE

The PEL tells us “how much”; the power profile tells us “when”

LoadSunEclipsePeak
OBC/C&DH8 W8 W10 W
ADCS121020
Payload35050
Comms5545

  • Do not add every nameplate rating and call it the peak: not all loads operate simultaneously.
  • Build explicit mission modes: safe, science, downlink, maneuver, eclipse, launch.
  • Transient loads can dominate switch/current sizing even when their energy is small.
Keep sunlight, eclipse and peak loads as separate columns: average power comes from the PEL, peak power from the power profile [1].
7 / 54
Study notes

The power equipment list (PEL) gives a number for each item in each condition. Notice that thermal is the largest eclipse load (20 W) although it is small in sunlight. The figure under the table is a real power profile built from a CubeSat PEL: a peak near 97 W for about 8 minutes on a baseline near 20 W [1].

Add the Sun column and you get 65 W. Add the Eclipse column and you get 43 W. Add the Peak column and you get 150 W, a number that never occurs, because the loads do not all peak together.

Check yourself. Why is the sum of the Peak column the wrong number to size the bus?

It assumes every load is at its peak at the same instant. The real peak is the largest mode total, found from the mode table on the next slide.

8 / 54
Study notes

The mode table turns the PEL into totals that actually occur. The OBC/C&DH draws 8 W in every mode, which is why the stacked bars are 8 W taller than the four columns of the table. The peak mode is downlink at 73 W, even though the payload is off.

Worked example. Eclipse mode draws 43 W. A 34-minute eclipse uses 43 × 34 ÷ 60 = 24.4 Wh, which the battery must supply.
Check yourself. In safe mode the ADCS load rises from 6 W to 14 W. What is the new safe-mode total?

8 + 14 + 0 + 2 + 12 = 36 W.

Slide 9
1 · MISSION MODES

A power budget is really an operations budget

Science modePayload dominates; ADCS may need precise pointing.
Downlink modeRF amplifier creates a high peak; payload may be off.
Safe modeMinimize load; preserve battery and thermal survival.
9 / 54
Study notes

This chart is the mode table laid out in time for one orbit. The green line is what the array produces (about 105 W in sunlight, zero in eclipse). The dark line is the load. The green area between them charges the battery. The red area in eclipse is taken out of the battery.

The figure on the right is a flight-design example: array power through one orbit for three orbit geometries [1]. Real generation is not a clean square wave.

Worked example. Surplus in sunlight = (105 − 65) × 42 ÷ 60 + (105 − 73) × 20 ÷ 60 = 28.0 + 10.7 = 38.7 Wh. Eclipse needs 24.4 Wh, so the orbit closes with room for storage losses.

1 · SOURCE SELECTION

Choose the source from mission duration, location and power level

SourceWhere it fitsWhat drives the trade
Primary batteryHours–daysStored energy, shelf life, mass
Fuel cellDaysReactant mass, peak power, water/heat
Photovoltaic + batteryMonths–yearsSunlight, eclipse, pointing, degradation

Mission-design rule: source selection is not a component preference. It follows from destination, duration, load profile, eclipse/illumination and acceptable risk.
Hardware images: [1].
10 / 54
Study notes

The source is chosen from how long the mission lasts, how much power it needs and how far it is from the Sun. The map shows the regions where each source is normally used; the boundaries are indicative [2]. Solar arrays with a battery cover most Earth-orbiting missions. RTGs take over where sunlight is weak and the mission lasts years.

Check yourself. Which source would you expect for (a) a two-week crewed vehicle needing several kW, (b) a ten-year 300 W mission to Saturn?

(a) Fuel cells. (b) An RTG.

Slide 11
1 · MISSION TRADE

Solar power remains viable far from the Sun — but area grows quickly

\[G(r)=\frac{G_{1AU}}{r_{AU}^2}\]
  • At Mars (~1.52 AU): ~43% of Earth-orbit solar flux.
  • At Jupiter (~5.2 AU): ~3.7%.
  • Low flux pushes array area, deployment complexity, structural dynamics and pointing into the mission architecture.
  • This is why source selection cannot be separated from destination.
Mars receives 43 % of Earth’s flux, Jupiter 3.7 %, Saturn 1.1 %.
11 / 54
Study notes

Solar flux falls with the square of the distance from the Sun. On log axes this is a straight line of slope −2: ten times farther gives one hundred times less flux. The array area for a given power grows by the same factor.

Worked example. At 2.8 AU the flux is 1361 ÷ 2.8² = 174 W/m². The array must be 2.8² = 7.8 times larger than at Earth for the same power.
Slide 12
1 · SOLAR CELLS

A solar cell is a converter with a maximum-power operating point

  • Photons create electron–hole pairs across a p–n junction.
  • Cell voltage falls as temperature rises; current rises slightly.
  • The product V×I has a maximum: MPPT keeps the array near this point.
  • Series cells set voltage; parallel strings set current and provide fault tolerance.
Cell types and efficiencies: [1].
12 / 54
Study notes

Sunlight enters through the coverglass, which also shields the cell from radiation. A photon absorbed in the cell creates an electron and a hole. The built-in field at the p–n junction pushes the electron to the front contact and the hole to the back, which drives current through the load.

One cell gives a low voltage. Cells in series add voltage to reach the bus level. Strings in parallel add current, and the array still works if one string fails. Space arrays mostly use triple-junction cells at about 29.5 % efficiency [1].

Slide 13
1 · SOLAR CELLS

The I–V curve explains why maximum-power tracking exists

  • At short circuit, voltage is nearly zero: high current but almost no useful power.
  • At open circuit, current is zero: high voltage but again no power.
  • The useful operating point lies at the maximum of V×I.
  • Temperature, radiation and illumination move the curve, so the optimum operating voltage also moves.
\[P_{mp}=V_{mp}I_{mp}\]
The I–V and P–V curves motivate the distinction between direct-energy-transfer and peak-power-tracking architectures [2].
13 / 54
Study notes

The green curve is current against voltage. At the left end (short circuit) the current is highest but the voltage is zero. At the right end (open circuit) the voltage is highest but the current is zero. Power is V × I, so it is zero at both ends and has a maximum at the knee: the maximum power point (MPP). The shaded rectangle is that maximum power.

Temperature, radiation and illumination move the whole curve, so the MPP moves too. That is why some systems track it (slide 34).

Check yourself. Why does a solar cell deliver no power at open circuit?

No current flows, and power is voltage × current.

Slide 14
1 · ENVIRONMENT

Solar-array output is a mission-environment quantity

Distance from SunFlux scales approximately as 1/r².
TemperatureHotter cells lose voltage and therefore power.
RadiationDisplacement damage reduces EOL output.
Angle of incidenceProjected input scales approximately with cos θ.
Packing & wiringNot all panel area is active cell; diodes/lines/converters lose power.
Mission lifeAll degradation accumulates to the EOL design point.
What the array actually faces on orbit. Images: [1].
14 / 54
Study notes

What an array delivers depends on where it is and for how long. The six tiles are the six corrections you apply to the rated output. The photographs show what the environment does in practice: charged particles, atomic-oxygen erosion of exposed materials, arcing between strings, hypervelocity impacts, and the loss of projected area when the Sun is off-normal [1].

Slide 15
1 · DEGRADATION

Temperature and radiation move the array away from its BOL rating

Measured trend for two triple-junction cell types, redrawn from [1].
  • Higher cell temperature primarily reduces voltage; power falls even if current rises slightly.
  • Radiation damage lowers output over mission life; the array must therefore close at end of life.
  • Coverglass reduces radiation dose but adds mass: thicker glass is traded against a smaller active-cell area.
\[P_{EOL}=P_{BOL}\,f_T\,f_{rad}\,f_{contam}\,f_{other}\]
15 / 54
Study notes

Compare the three curves. A hot cell loses open-circuit voltage and gains a little current, so its power falls. Radiation at end of life lowers both current and voltage. The dots show how the maximum power point moves down and to the left.

The lower chart is measured data for two triple-junction cell types: about −0.2 W per °C, or −0.25 % per °C [1].

Worked example. An array gives 80 W at 28 °C. At 78 °C it is 50 °C hotter, so it loses 50 × 0.25 % = 12.5 %. Output = 80 × 0.875 = 70 W.
Slide 16
1 · EOL DESIGN

Design the array for end of life, not beginning of life

\[P_{EPS}/A=G_s\,\eta_{cell}\,f_T\,f_{EOL}\,f_{pack}\,\cos\theta\,\eta_{path}\]

The worked example in [1] uses 1366.1 W/m², 28.3% cell efficiency, 0.88 temperature factor, 0.93 EOL environment, 0.90 packing, 0.99 AOI and 0.85 path efficiency, giving about 239.6 W/m² delivered to EPS.

Why EOL?

If a five-year spacecraft only closes its budget at BOL, it does not have a five-year power system.

Growth margin and designer’s margin are added after the physics/loss factors.

16 / 54
Study notes

The equation multiplies the sunlight by every loss factor to give the power delivered to the EPS per square metre at end of life (EOL). The waterfall shows the same chain one step at a time. Only 17.5 % of the incident sunlight reaches the bus. The result, 239.6 W/m², is the design value used in the array-sizing examples later.

Worked example. With a cell efficiency of 0.30 the chain gives 1366.1 × 0.30 × 0.88 × 0.93 × 0.90 × 0.99 × 0.85 = 254 W/m².
Check yourself. Why is the budget closed at end of life and not at launch?

The array is weakest at end of life. A design that closes only at launch does not have power for the whole mission.

Slide 17
CASE STUDY · SOLAR AT JUPITER

Juno shows what \(1/r^2\) means at spacecraft scale

  • Jupiter receives roughly 1/25 of the sunlight available near Earth.
  • Juno therefore uses three very large solar wings; each is about 2.65 m × 8.9 m.
  • The three arrays deliver about 450 W of electrical power at Jupiter.
  • The EPS also includes two 55 Ah Li-ion batteries for off-Sun/eclipsed operation.
\[G(5.2\,AU)\approx \frac{1361}{5.2^2}\approx 50\;W/m^2\]
Juno solar-array deployment test. Image: NASA/JPL-Caltech/Lockheed Martin.
17 / 54
Study notes

Juno is the 1/r² law at full scale. At 5.2 AU the flux is about 50 W/m², one twenty-fifth of Earth's, so three wings of about 2.65 m × 8.9 m deliver only about 450 W. The squares show the array area for the same power at Earth, Mars and Jupiter.

Slide 18
1 · BATTERIES

Energy storage bridges the gap between generation and demand

\[E_{ecl}=\frac{P_{ecl}\,t_{ecl}}{\eta_d\eta_b}\]
\[C_{rated}\ge \frac{E_{ecl}}{DOD_{max}}\]
  • Depth of discharge (DOD) trades battery mass against cycle life.
  • LEO can impose thousands of shallow cycles per year; GEO has fewer but longer seasonal eclipses.
  • Battery temperature is an EPS–thermal interface: performance, charge acceptance and life are temperature dependent.
  • Charge control and state-of-charge knowledge are mission-critical.
18 / 54
Study notes

The first equation is the energy taken from the battery in eclipse: load power × eclipse time, divided by the discharge efficiencies. The second gives the rated capacity: that energy divided by the largest depth of discharge (DOD) you allow.

In the chart the state of charge rises in sunlight, stays full, then falls in eclipse. The height of each fall is the DOD.

Slide 19
1 · BATTERY DESIGN

Battery sizing is an energy problem constrained by life

\[E_{load}=P_{ecl}t_{ecl}\]
\[E_{battery,rated}\ge \frac{E_{load}}{\eta_{dis}\,DOD_{max}}\]
  • Lower allowable DOD means a larger battery but generally improves cycle life.
  • LEO can impose thousands of cycles per year, so DOD is a lifetime variable, not just a sizing knob.
  • Peak power can independently constrain cell count because cells have current limits.
InSight Mars lander battery assembly (EaglePicher). Hardware reminds us that storage includes cells, structure, harnessing, sensing and protection.
19 / 54
Study notes

A battery is sized for energy and then checked for life and for current. The pack diagram shows how cells are arranged: the number in series sets the voltage, and the number of strings in parallel sets the capacity and the current.

Worked example. Eclipse load 43 W for 34 minutes, discharge efficiency 0.90, maximum DOD 30 %. Load energy = 24.4 Wh. From the battery = 24.4 ÷ 0.90 = 27.1 Wh. Rated capacity = 27.1 ÷ 0.30 = 90 Wh.
Check yourself. A 28 V bus uses 3.6 V, 3 Ah Li-ion cells and needs 20 Ah. How many cells?

Series: 28 ÷ 3.6 = 7.8, so 8. Parallel: 20 ÷ 3 = 6.7, so 7 strings. Total 56 cells.

Slide 20
1 · BATTERY LIFE

Depth of discharge is a mission-life trade

  • The exact curve depends on chemistry, temperature, C-rate and qualification data.
  • The design question is therefore: what DOD can the mission afford for the required number of eclipse cycles?
  • A battery sized only from Wh, without cycle-life reasoning, is not a mission design.
This is why orbit selection and EPS design are coupled: eclipse frequency and duration become battery life and mass.
20 / 54
Study notes

The deeper each discharge, the fewer cycles a battery survives. The curve is an illustrative trend for Li-ion; real designs use the cell maker's qualification data. A LEO mission needs tens of thousands of cycles, so only about 20 to 30 % DOD is affordable. A GEO mission needs about a thousand, so 60 to 80 % is possible.

Worked example. A 95-minute orbit gives 525,960 ÷ 95 = 5536 eclipses a year. Over 3 years the battery sees about 16,600 cycles.

Storage technology is a system trade, not just Wh/kg

Table and curves redrawn from [1]; current flight cells vary by vendor and qualification.
21 / 54
Study notes

The table and the two charts compare chemistries [1]. Li-ion stores the most energy per kilogram (130 Wh/kg, almost four times Ni-Cd) and has the highest cell voltage (3.6 V), so fewer cells are needed in series. Its cycle life depends on keeping the depth of discharge under control.

24 / 54
Study notes

The orbit is split into four segments. For each, the energy change is (generation − load) × time. Science removes 1.15 Wh even in sunlight. Eclipse removes 2.25 Wh. The two low-power sunlit segments put back more than both, so the net is +13.7 Wh and the orbit is power-positive.

The design closes when the net energy is positive, the state of charge stays above the minimum, and the orbit margin meets the target.

Try it. Lengthen the science segment until the net energy per orbit turns negative. How many minutes of science can this design afford?
Slide 25
PADRE · DISCUSSION

What does the PADRE model teach us?

Eclipse time drives storageBattery energy grows almost linearly with eclipse duration.
DOD is a life tradeAllowing deeper DOD shrinks battery capacity, but generally increases cycling stress.
Losses hit twiceStorage inefficiency increases both battery energy removed and daytime recharge power.
Margin is expensiveA 20–30% growth/design allowance directly increases array area.
Thermal couples backCold-case heater power can make eclipse load exceed sunlit load.
Operations can fix hardwareTurning payloads off in eclipse may save more mass than improving cell efficiency.
25 / 54
Study notes

Each tile is something you can see in the model. Lengthen the eclipse and the battery need grows. Allow a deeper discharge and the battery shrinks but ages faster. Storage losses count twice: once when discharging and again when recharging. Turning a payload off in eclipse can save more mass than a better solar cell.

Slide 26
1 · ARRAY SIZING

The solar array must run the spacecraft and repay the eclipse energy

\[P_{SA}=\frac{1}{\eta_r}\left(P_{sun}+\frac{P_{ecl}t_{ecl}}{\eta_{storage}\,t_{sun}}\right)\]
  • First term: operate sunlit loads.
  • Second term: recharge what the battery supplied during eclipse.
  • Then apply EOL cell performance, packing, incidence, regulation and margin to convert required power into area.
The required area has to exist on the spacecraft. Images: [1].
26 / 54
Study notes

The array has two jobs in sunlight. The gold block is the sunlit load. The green block on top is the power needed to put back what the battery supplied in eclipse, including the storage loss. The array must deliver the sum.

Worked example. Sunlit load 120 W; eclipse load 144 W for 30 min; sunlight 66 min; storage efficiency 0.82. Recharge power = 144 × 30 ÷ (0.82 × 66) = 79.8 W. Array power to the bus = 120 + 79.8 = 200 W.
Check yourself. Sunlit load 65 W, eclipse load 43 W for 34 min, sunlight 62 min, storage efficiency 0.82. Find the array power.

Recharge = 43 × 34 ÷ (0.82 × 62) = 28.8 W. Array = 65 + 28.8 = 93.8 W.

Slide 27
1 · MARGIN

Margins protect against uncertainty; they do not replace a missing budget

Growth margin

Allows loads to mature as design proceeds.

Design margin

Provides robustness against residual uncertainty and implementation losses.

Keep margins visible as separate factors. Hiding them inside efficiency numbers makes the design impossible to audit.
27 / 54
Study notes

Margins are added to the best estimate as separate lines so that anyone can audit them. The bar shows the example from [1]: 120 W of load, plus 20 % growth margin, converted to area, plus 10 % designer's margin.

Worked example. 120 W × 1.20 = 144 W. Area = 144 ÷ 239.6 = 0.601 m². With 10 % designer's margin: 0.661 m².

Slide 31
2 · ARCHITECTURE

EPS has four jobs: generate, store, transmit, regulate/protect

The same four-block decomposition is used in [1]. It is a useful mission-design abstraction before selecting hardware.
31 / 54
Study notes

Follow the power from left to right. The solar array produces unregulated DC. The array regulator either shunts the excess or tracks the maximum power point. The main bus feeds the loads and, through the charge and discharge control, the battery. DC/DC converters give each load its voltage. Distribution switches and protects each branch. Telemetry from every block goes to the on-board computer.

Check yourself. Name the four jobs of an EPS.

Generate, store, regulate and distribute (with protection).

Slide 32
2 · BUS VOLTAGE

Bus voltage is an architecture trade

Higher voltageLower current for the same power → smaller conductor losses and potentially lighter wiring.
Lower voltageSimpler interfaces for small loads, but higher current at high power.
Regulated vs unregulatedRegulated bus simplifies loads; unregulated can reduce conversion stages but pushes voltage variation downstream.
\[P=VI,\qquad P_{wire}=I^2R\]
32 / 54
Study notes

Bus voltage is a design choice. A higher voltage carries the same power with less current, which reduces harness loss. The chart shows the second choice. An unregulated bus follows the battery voltage up in sunlight and down in eclipse, and every load must tolerate the swing. A regulated bus stays constant, at the cost of an extra converter stage and its loss.

Slide 33
2 · DISTRIBUTION

Higher bus voltage can save harness mass

\[I=\frac{P}{V}\]
\[P_{wire}=I^2R=\frac{P^2R}{V^2}\]

For the same delivered power, doubling bus voltage halves current and reduces a fixed-resistance harness loss by a factor of four.

But voltage is not free

Higher voltage changes insulation, connector spacing, converter design, fault energy and component availability.

Mission-design trade: harness mass/loss versus conversion and high-voltage implementation risk.

33 / 54
Study notes

For a fixed power, current is P ÷ V and harness loss is I²R, so loss falls with the square of the bus voltage. The chart is for 100 W through 0.1 Ω: 40 W lost at 5 V, 1.3 W at 28 V.

Check yourself. A 0.2 Ω harness carries 60 W. Find the loss at 5 V and at 12 V.

At 5 V: 12 A, loss 28.8 W. At 12 V: 5 A, loss 5.0 W.

Slide 34
2 · DET VS MPPT

Two common ways to couple the array to the bus

Direct Energy Transfer (DET)

Array is tied more directly to the bus; excess power is shunted/dissipated. Simple and common at lower power.

Peak/Maximum Power Point Tracking

A converter dynamically holds the array near maximum power. Gains energy harvest but adds conversion loss, control and complexity.

DET shunts unused power, while peak-power trackers dynamically change the array operating point and consume several percent of array power [2].
34 / 54
Study notes

Both charts show the same array when cold and when hot. With direct energy transfer (DET) the bus voltage fixes where the array operates, so a cold array (high voltage) leaves power unused. With peak-power tracking (MPPT) a converter moves the operating point to the knee of whichever curve applies, and pays several per cent in converter loss [2].

Check yourself. When is MPPT worth its converter loss?

When array temperature or illumination varies widely, so a fixed bus voltage would sit far from the maximum power point for much of the time.

Slide 35
2 · REGULATION

DET and MPPT solve the same problem differently

Direct Energy Transfer (DET), unregulated bus

Simple; array/bus operating point is constrained. DET/shunt approaches are common for lower-power systems [2].

Peak-power tracker (PPT / MPPT), regulated bus

Converter actively holds the array near MPP as illumination and temperature change, at the cost of converter mass/loss/control complexity.

Topologies redrawn after [1].
35 / 54
Study notes

Find the differences between the two diagrams. In DET the array reaches the bus through a diode, a shunt regulator dumps excess power as heat, and the battery sits directly on the bus. In the peak-power tracker the array reaches the bus through a converter, and the battery has its own charger and discharger. Both end in the same regulator, distribution and loads [1].

Slide 36
2 · DISTRIBUTION

Power distribution is where failures become system failures

  • Switch loads with mechanical or solid-state relays.
  • Use current limiting/fuses and redundant paths where required.
  • Isolate faults so one load cannot collapse the bus.
  • Account for inrush, transient loads and harness voltage drop.
  • Measure bus voltage/current and critical branch currents for FDIR.
36 / 54
Study notes

Each load has its own switch and current limiter (LCL). When one branch short-circuits, its limiter opens and the bus keeps its voltage for the other loads. Currents are measured on every branch for fault detection. The figure on the left is a real CubeSat EPS: 4 V panels, a boost converter, a battery charger and four buck converters [1].

Slide 37
2 · CONVERTERS

Every conversion stage is also a thermal load

\[P_{loss}=P_{in}-P_{out}=P_{out}\left(\frac{1}{\eta}-1\right)\]

A 100 W load behind a 90% efficient converter requires 111 W from the bus and dissipates ~11 W as heat.

  • Buck, boost and buck/boost topologies serve different input/output ranges.
  • Linear regulators are simple but can waste substantial power when voltage drop and current are large.
  • Worst-case steady and transient load, radiation, temperature, stability and EMI all enter converter selection.
37 / 54
Study notes

A converter that is 90 % efficient turns the other 10 % into heat inside the spacecraft. Efficiencies along a path multiply. In the chart, 0.99 × 0.99 × 0.88 × 0.99 = 0.854, so 100 W from the array becomes 85.4 W at the loads [1].

Check yourself. The path efficiency is 0.854. How much array power is needed for 50 W at the loads, and how much heat is produced?

50 ÷ 0.854 = 58.5 W. Heat = 8.5 W.

Slide 38
2 · BATTERY CONTROL

Battery management is power, thermal and operations engineering at once

BMUMonitors voltage, current, temperature and cell health; estimates state of charge.
Charge regulatorControls recharge in sunlight; Li-ion commonly uses constant-current then constant-voltage behavior.
Discharge pathSupports the bus in eclipse or when source power is insufficient; must protect against undervoltage and overcurrent.
38 / 54
Study notes

The left chart is a Li-ion charge: constant current until the cell reaches 4.2 V, then constant voltage while the current tapers. The right chart is a discharge: a quick drop (A), a long flat plateau (B) and a knee (C). Because the plateau is flat, voltage alone is a poor fuel gauge, and loads are shed before the knee.

Slide 39
2 · RELIABILITY

Derating and protection are part of EPS sizing

  • Size switches, converters and wiring for worst-case steady and transient conditions — not nominal only.
  • Protect against shorts, overvoltage, undervoltage, reverse current and ESD.
  • Solar arrays are mechanically vulnerable; batteries contain significant stored energy.
  • Parts grade and radiation tolerance are mission-environment decisions.
Mission-design question

What single-point EPS failure can end the mission? What redundancy or graceful degradation is justified by mission value, cost and mass?

39 / 54
Study notes

Parts are run below their ratings because failure rate rises with temperature and with stress ratio, as the left figure shows [3]. The diode figures show two protections on the array. Blocking diodes stop a failed or shadowed string from drawing current from the others. Bypass diodes carry current around a shaded cell so it does not limit the whole string [4].

Slide 40
2 · RTG

When sunlight is the wrong resource: RTGs

  • Radioactive decay supplies continuous heat; thermoelectrics convert a small fraction to electricity.
  • Power is independent of sunlight, pointing and eclipse.
  • Pu-238’s long half-life supports long missions; about 96% of the thermal output remains after five years from decay alone [2].
  • Electrical conversion efficiency is low, so waste heat becomes a major thermal-design input.
Systems coupling

RTG → continuous electrical power + large continuous waste heat + radiation/placement constraints.

This is why EPS source selection changes structures, thermal design, payload accommodation and operations.

40 / 54
Study notes

A radioisotope thermoelectric generator (RTG) turns decay heat into electricity. Its output does not depend on sunlight, pointing or eclipse. On the chart, the thermal output falls slowly with the 87.7-year half-life of Pu-238. The electrical output falls faster because the thermocouples also age; that curve is indicative.

Slide 41
2 · RTG SYSTEMS

An RTG is primarily a heat source with a small electrical output

\[\eta_{RTG}=\frac{P_{electric}}{Q_{thermal}}\]
  • Conventional RTG conversion efficiency is only about 5% [2].
  • Therefore most decay energy appears as heat that must be rejected or deliberately used for spacecraft warming.
  • RTG placement can be driven by thermal and instrument-interference considerations as much as by wiring.
41 / 54
Study notes

Only about 5 % of the heat becomes electricity [2]. The rest must be radiated to space or used to keep the spacecraft warm. The band widths in the diagram are proportional to the energy flow.

Check yourself. An RTG delivers 285 W of electricity at 5 % efficiency. Estimate its thermal power and its waste heat.

Thermal = 285 ÷ 0.05 = 5700 W. Waste heat = 5415 W.

Slide 42
2 · DEEP SPACE

Solar vs RTG becomes a mission-architecture trade with distance

\[G(r)\approx \frac{1361}{r_{AU}^2}\;W/m^2\]
  • At 5.2 AU (Jupiter), solar flux is only ~3.7% of Earth’s.
  • Large solar arrays remain possible for some outer-planet missions, but area, deployment, pointing and low-temperature operation become major trades.
  • RTGs remove Sun-pointing and eclipse dependence but introduce low efficiency, cost and nuclear-safety constraints.
42 / 54
Study notes

The chart shows the array area needed for 300 W at each planet, using 239.6 W/m² at 1 AU and the 1/r² law only. About 1.3 m² at Earth becomes 34 m² at Jupiter and 114 m² at Saturn. An RTG gives the same power at any distance, which is why the choice of source depends on the destination.

Slide 43
INTERACTIVE CASE B · SETUP

Case B workflow — continuous source, scheduled loads

Outer-planet science probe

Long cruise · low sunlight · continuous housekeeping · science campaigns · high-power telecom peaks.

  • Close the budget at EOL encounter, not launch.
  • Schedule science/downlink duty cycles below average source capability.
  • Use storage only where peak demand exceeds continuous source output.
Power-positive on average (164 W < 210 W) yet the 312 W peak still needs about 17 Wh from a buffer battery.
43 / 54
Study notes

Case B is a probe powered by one RTG. The green line is what the RTG supplies at end of life: 210 W, all day. The dark line is the load through an illustrative day. For most of the day the load is below the line. During the telecom peak it is above the line, and a battery must supply the red area.

Check yourself. The average demand is below the RTG output. Why is a battery still needed?

The average says nothing about the instant. During the peak the load exceeds what the RTG can supply.

CASE B · DISCUSSION

What changes when generation is continuous but limited?

No eclipse recharge problemThe RTG generates continuously, so the battery is mainly a peak/transient buffer rather than an orbital-night reservoir.
Operations become a leverScience and downlink duty cycles can be scheduled so average demand stays below EOL source power.
EOL still rulesA mission that closes at launch but not at encounter is not closed.
Waste heat is valuable and dangerousRTG thermal power can warm the bus but may disturb instruments or require placement away from the spacecraft.
Source count is discreteOne more RTG is a large step in mass, cost and heat — unlike adding a small strip of solar cells.
Storage still mattersHigh-power transmitters or mechanisms may need a battery/capacitor even with continuous generation.
46 / 54
Study notes

Compare with the PADRE case. There is no eclipse, so the battery is a buffer for peaks. The schedule (duty cycles) is the main design lever. The budget must still close at end of life. The waste heat is both useful and a constraint, and adding a second RTG is a large step, unlike adding a few solar cells.

2 · SYSTEM TRADE

The same mission requirement can produce very different EPS architectures

DriverLEO solar/batteryOuter-planet RTG
Generation variabilityStrong orbit-cycleContinuous, slowly declining
Storage roleEclipse + peaksPeaks/transients
Attitude couplingSolar incidence mattersWeak for generation
Thermal couplingCell temperature + heatersLarge continuous waste heat
EOL driverRadiation, temperature, contaminationSource/thermocouple degradation

Study notes

The table sets the two cases side by side, and the sketches show the difference in one picture: a LEO array switches on and off every orbit, while an RTG gives a flat, slowly falling output with short load peaks above it.

Slide 48
2 · MAKE OR BUY

Make/buy is a mission trade: cost × risk × benefit × schedule

  • COTS EPS can reduce schedule and non-recurring engineering.
  • Custom design can improve efficiency, packaging and interfaces.
  • Flight heritage is valuable only if the new mission environment and loads remain inside the qualified envelope.
  • Procurement lead time, radiation assurance and acceptance testing belong in the early design.
Mission design

A “perfect” custom converter delivered after integration is worse than a slightly less efficient qualified unit available on schedule.

48 / 54
Study notes

Buying a commercial EPS saves time and engineering. A custom design can be more efficient. Flight heritage only helps if the new mission stays inside the environment and loads the unit was qualified for.

Slide 49
2 · VERIFICATION

Verification must reproduce the electrical states that matter

Solar arraysThermal cycling · deployment · UV/AO characterization · continuity · photovoltaic aliveness.
BatteriesCapacity · charge retention · thermal cycling · vacuum/leak checks · abuse tolerance.
PCDU / convertersMin/max input voltage · min/max load · transients · protection · EMI · continuity/isolation.
Qualification and acceptance testing are tailored to EPS component risks, followed by system-level functional checks after final installation [1].
Each level re-uses measured data from the one below; the budget is re-run with measured efficiencies.
49 / 54
Study notes

Testing builds up in levels, from parts to the whole spacecraft, and each level uses measured data from the one below. The tiles list the tests that are specific to arrays, batteries and converters [1]. Deployment is a one-shot event in flight, so large arrays are deployed on the ground first.

Slide 50
2 · VERIFICATION

Verification closes the EPS model against hardware

  1. Component: cell/array I–V, battery capacity, converter efficiency, protection thresholds.
  2. Subsystem: min/max bus voltage, peak load, charge/discharge, fault isolation, deployment.
  3. Spacecraft: execute real modes and transitions with representative loads and thermal states.
  4. Correlate: replace assumed efficiencies/degradation with measured values and re-run the EOL budget.
The budget is not verified because each box works independently. It is verified when the integrated spacecraft can execute the mission profile with margin.
Juno after spacecraft thermal-vacuum testing; solar-array simulators reproduced array thermal properties. Image: NASA/JPL-Caltech/Lockheed Martin.
50 / 54
Study notes

The four steps go from components to the integrated spacecraft. The last step is the one that proves the budget: assumed efficiencies and degradation are replaced by measured values, and the end-of-life budget is run again.

Slide 51
2 · INTEGRATION

Close the EPS at spacecraft level, not component level

  • Re-run the power budget whenever operations, thermal heater power, payload duty cycle or comms plan changes.
  • Check safe mode separately: can the spacecraft remain power-positive and recover?
  • Check peak current and energy separately.
  • Track margin through design maturity instead of treating it as spare power to spend.
Definition of “power positive”

Over the relevant cycle, generated energy exceeds consumed energy after losses, while instantaneous source/storage capability meets every peak.

51 / 54
Study notes

The chain lists everything that enters the budget, and the dashed arrow says it is re-run with measured values. Learn the definition of power-positive: over the cycle, generated energy exceeds consumed energy after losses, and the source plus storage can meet every peak. Safe mode is checked separately.

SUMMARY

Electrical power system design in one page

Power ≠ energyPeaks size current paths; time-integrated demand sizes storage/generation.
Design at EOLTemperature, radiation, cycling and degradation are mission variables.
Operations are hardwareDuty cycle and mode scheduling can close a budget without adding mass.
EPS is coupledThermal heaters, attitude, comms, payload and orbit all change the answer.
Protect the busFault isolation and derating preserve the mission when hardware fails.
Verify the real statesTest min/max voltage, load, transients, storage and deployment behavior.

54 / 54
Study notes

Reference numbers in these notes, such as [1] and [2], point to this list.

Practice problems

Sixteen problems in the order of the lecture. Use 1361 W/m² at 1 AU and 239.6 W/m² delivered at end of life unless told otherwise. Click a problem to see its answer.

Power, energy and modes

1. A 45 W transmitter runs for 12 minutes in each 96-minute orbit. Find its energy per orbit and its contribution to orbit-average power.

Energy = 45 × 12 ÷ 60 = 9 Wh. Average contribution = 45 × 12 ÷ 96 = 5.6 W.

2. In the mode table (slide 8) the safe-mode ADCS load rises from 6 W to 14 W. Find the new safe-mode total and the energy used in a 34-minute eclipse spent in safe mode.

Safe total = 8 + 14 + 0 + 2 + 12 = 36 W. Energy = 36 × 34 ÷ 60 = 20.4 Wh.

Sources and arrays

3. Find the solar flux at 2.8 AU. By what factor must the array area grow, compared with Earth orbit, for the same power?

Flux = 1361 ÷ 2.8² = 174 W/m². Area grows by 2.8² = 7.8.

4. Repeat the loss chain of slide 16 with a cell efficiency of 0.30.

1366.1 × 0.30 × 0.88 × 0.93 × 0.90 × 0.99 × 0.85 = 254 W/m².

5. An array delivers 80 W at 28 °C. Its power falls by 0.25 % per °C. Estimate its output at 78 °C.

50 °C hotter gives −12.5 %. Output = 80 × 0.875 = 70 W.

Storage

6. The eclipse load is 60 W for 35 minutes. Discharge efficiency is 0.90 and maximum DOD is 25 %. Find the rated battery capacity and the cell mass at 130 Wh/kg.

Load energy = 35 Wh. From the battery = 38.9 Wh. Capacity = 38.9 ÷ 0.25 = 156 Wh. Mass = 1.2 kg.

7. A spacecraft is in a 95-minute orbit for 3 years with one eclipse per orbit. How many charge cycles does the battery see?

525,960 ÷ 95 = 5536 per year, about 16,600 in 3 years.

8. A 28 V bus uses 3.6 V Li-ion cells of 3 Ah. The battery must hold 20 Ah. How many cells in series, strings in parallel and cells in total?

8 in series, 7 strings in parallel, 56 cells.

Array sizing and margins

9. Sunlit load 65 W. Eclipse load 43 W for 34 minutes. Sunlight 62 minutes. Storage efficiency 0.82. Find the array power to the bus. Then add 20 % growth margin, convert to area at 239.6 W/m², and add 10 % designer's margin.

Recharge = 43 × 34 ÷ (0.82 × 62) = 28.8 W. Array = 93.8 W. With growth = 112.5 W, area 0.470 m². With designer's margin = 0.517 m².

Architecture

10. A harness of 0.2 Ω carries 60 W. Find the harness loss at a 5 V bus and at a 12 V bus.

At 5 V: 12 A, 28.8 W. At 12 V: 5 A, 5.0 W.

11. The path from array to loads has a total efficiency of 0.854. How much array power is needed for 50 W at the loads, and how much heat is produced?

58.5 W from the array; 8.5 W of heat.

12. Explain in two sentences when peak-power tracking is worth its converter loss.

When array temperature or illumination varies widely, a fixed bus voltage sits far from the maximum power point. Tracking pays when the power recovered exceeds the converter loss of several per cent.

The two cases

13. PADRE: only 80 of the 96 cells face the Sun. Find the EOL array power, and the energy the battery supplies during a 28-minute science segment at 40.84 W.

Array = 80 × 1.107 × 0.361 = 32.0 W. Deficit = 8.9 W for 28 min = 4.1 Wh.

14. Case B: the science duty cycle rises from 0.25 to 0.40. The other loads average 143.96 W in total. Find the new total average demand and the margin left after 20 %, at 210 W end-of-life power.

Science = 5 × 0.60 + 65 × 0.40 = 29 W. Total = 172.96 W. With margin = 207.55 W. Left = 2.45 W. It closes, barely.

15. An RTG delivers 285 W of electricity at 5 % efficiency. Estimate its thermal power and its waste heat.

Thermal = 5700 W. Waste heat = 5415 W.

16. A classmate says: “The average budget closes with margin, so no battery is needed.” Explain why this is wrong for an RTG-powered probe.

The average says nothing about the instant. When the transmitter and science run together the load exceeds the RTG output, and only a battery can supply the difference.

Formula sheet

Energy\[E=\int P\,dt\]
Solar flux\[G(r)=\dfrac{1361}{r_{AU}^2}\ \mathrm{W/m^2}\]
Maximum power\[P_{mp}=V_{mp}I_{mp}\]
EOL power per area\[\dfrac{P_{EPS}}{A}=G_s\,\eta_{cell}\,f_T\,f_{EOL}\,f_{pack}\cos\theta\,\eta_{path}\]
Eclipse energy\[E_{ecl}=\dfrac{P_{ecl}\,t_{ecl}}{\eta_d\,\eta_b}\]
Battery capacity\[C_{rated}\ge\dfrac{E_{ecl}}{DOD_{max}}\]
Array power\[P_{SA}=\dfrac{1}{\eta_r}\left(P_{sun}+\dfrac{P_{ecl}\,t_{ecl}}{\eta_{storage}\,t_{sun}}\right)\]
Harness loss\[P_{wire}=I^2R=\dfrac{P^2R}{V^2}\]
Converter loss\[P_{loss}=P_{out}\left(\dfrac{1}{\eta}-1\right)\]
Orbit period\[T=2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{(R_E+h)^3}{\mu}}\]
Average of duty-cycled loads\[P_{avg}=\sum_i\left[P_{s,i}(1-D_i)+P_{a,i}D_i\right]\]
Buffer energy\[E_{buffer}=\max(0,\,P_{peak}-P_{EOL})\,t_{peak}\]

Glossary

EPSElectrical power system: generates, stores, regulates and distributes power.
PELPower equipment list: the power drawn by each item.
Power profileLoad against time over an orbit or a day.
BOL, EOLBeginning of life and end of life. Budgets are closed at EOL.
MPPMaximum power point: the knee of the I–V curve.
DET, MPPTDirect energy transfer; maximum (peak) power point tracking.
DODDepth of discharge: the fraction of battery capacity used in one cycle.
Duty cycleFraction of time a load is in its active state.
MarginAllowance added to the best-estimate load, kept as a separate line.
LCLLatching current limiter: a protected switch on one load branch.
DeratingRunning a part below its rating to lower its failure rate.
RTGRadioisotope thermoelectric generator.
Power-positiveEnergy generated over the cycle exceeds energy consumed, and every peak can be met.
